title: Load moved fixtures exactly as javac read them

blocks.text: The integration tests of the catalogue service kept their expected responses as text blocks, two hundred of them, and the test classes became unreadable. The team moved each block's body into a fixture file, byte for byte: everything after the line of the opening `"""`, up to the closing `"""`. Some bodies hold escapes, some hold Unicode escapes such as `\u00e9` that their authors used to keep the sources in ASCII, and the files are checked out with CRLF line endings on Windows.
A fixture is only useful if it loads as exactly the string the text block had. Finish the two `TODO`s in `src/main/java/practice/FixtureLoader.java`:

items: `unicodeEscapes(text)`: the text with each Unicode escape replaced by its character, as javac does when it reads a source file;
`load(body)`: the string javac made of a text block with this body.

blocks.text: When you're done, every fixture loads as the value javac gave its block, on Linux and on Windows. About fifteen lines in total.
The tests compare with values that javac 21 produced from the same bodies.

cases.says: a JSON fixture with CRLF line endings, an escape and relative indentation loads with LF endings, the escape interpreted and the indentation kept
a fixture whose closing delimiter followed its last line loads without a final line break
Unicode escapes become their characters, and an escaped backslash from one then starts an ordinary escape
spaces kept by \s and carriage returns written as \r are in the loaded value
a backslash written as \\ before a u stays a backslash followed by the letters
a line break written as a Unicode escape starts a new line before the indentation is measured

origin.section: translateEscapes() Interprets Escapes in a String That Arrives at Run Time

concepts: Reproducing a text block's value from its body means translating Unicode escapes first (an escaped backslash starts none), then stripping indentation, then interpreting escapes.
